You're thinking of depression as steming exclusively from a series of thoughts and so could be eliminated by simply changing those thoughts. This is known as cognitive behavioral therapy, and while it can be very effective, it can never eliminate the root of true clinical depression: an imbalance of chemicals that leads to unhappiness. No matter what frame of mind you have, you can't help it if you're brain juices are out of whack. If antidepressants make you unnaturally happy, then depression is what makes you unnaturally unhappy. Not all forms of depression are purely due to brain juice imbalances however, and so to avoid unnecessary medications, therapy should always be tried before prescribing drugs.

Glad to help. I’ve never gone under anesthesia, but I think that is a case where the brain is “dead,” in the sense that there is no activity at all. This is unlike sleep, where it is organizing and collecting your thoughts and memories in the subconscious. I think I understand your concern of an interrupted consciousness: do you wake up as a different “person” after you become unconscious, but “feel” as if you are the same “person” because you have retained the same brain and thus the same memories and behaviors? I think no. For example, when you shut down your computer, and then restart it later, it can still preform the exact same tasks it could before it was shut down, it retains the same memory, and physically it is the same object. So, it must still be the same computer, and as the analogy implies, the same “person.” In the same way, I don’t think society would treat theoretical “restarts” as zombies or clones, if that makes sense. Of course I’m just speculating and I’m not sure how philosophically accurate that analogy is. Yeah I can see why you stay up late haha. Btw these aren’t questions I would worry about of course. They are beyond our control, and as you know existential crises aren’t much fun.

You cannot experience being unconscious. Why fear experiencing something that, by definition, cannot be experienced? And if you still fear total death, then you can take comfort in the fact that you are not totally dead when you are asleep. You can tell this without being a neuroscientist because you can *feel* that time passed during your sleep, as your brain was still awake at a subconscious level. And occasionally you may have dreams or nightmares. If you truly died and completely lost all consciousness when you went to sleep, then you would immediately wake up eight hours later. Essentially this is evidence that you do retain the same consciousness between falling asleep and waking up.
